facts.value: A.2 Treasury Management Performance 2025/26, report of the Corporate Finance & Governance Portfolio Holder, to Cabinet on Friday 24 July 2026. Eleven-page covering report (doc 82606) plus a five-page Prudential and Treasury Indicators pack as Appendix B (doc 82608). Both on disk. Appendix A (Treasury Performance figures 2025/26) is listed on p11 and referenced in the main body (SONIA benchmark table quoted at p7 and £1.5077bn aggregate investment figure at p8 both said to sit in Appendix A) but is not on disk — however the SONIA table and aggregate figure are both restated in the main body text, so absence of Appendix A does not leave a hole in the reconciliation. Report Contact Officer is Richard Barrett, Corporate Director (Finance and IT), rbarrett@tendringdc.gov.uk, 01255 686521, printed on p11. The Section 151 Officer sign-off box on p4 says verbatim: 'The Section 151 Officer is the author of this report.' — i.e. the report author IS the S151. The paper does not literally state 'Richard Barrett is the Section 151 Officer' anywhere; combining the sign-off with the Report Contact Officer block makes Richard Barrett the S151 by inference. Title is taken verbatim as Corporate Director (Finance and IT). Read in full from local PDFs on 2026-08-16.

source.title: A.2 Treasury Management Performance 2025/26 — Cabinet 24 July 2026

facts.note: S151 identity is inferred, not stated. Officer title stays verbatim as 'Corporate Director (Finance and IT)' in the recipient line.

facts.value: TIES to the pound AND to the basis point. Our file at 2026-03-31 for borrower TENDRING DISTRICT COUNCIL: 17 loans, £28,232,443 principal, weighted rate 3.6053%, mix 6 ANNUITY / 7 MATURITY / 4 EIP. Paper Executive Summary (p1) splits the same book as General Fund £0.112m @ 6.884% + Housing Revenue Account £28.120m @ 3.591%. Total principal £28.232m — ties to the pound. Blended weighted rate: (0.112 × 6.884 + 28.120 × 3.591) / 28.232 = 3.6053%, ties to the basis point. Appendix B p2 restates external debt at 31/3/26 as £28,232k. Additionally the maturity-profile bucket cross-checks to the pound: Appendix B p5 shows 53.13% of the book in the 20–30 year bucket = 53.13% × £28,232k = £15,000,000 exactly, and our file's '25 years and over' bucket holds £15,000,000 across 6 loans. The paper does not print a loan count in the body or in Appendix B; count of 17 is ours. Safe to quote in the email as '17 PWLB loans totalling £28,232,443 at a weighted 3.6053%' — count is ours, principal and weighted rate both tie.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py --find and --as-at; paper Executive Summary (p1); Appendix B p2 and p5

facts.note: Strongest reconciliation we've had in the batch. Principal to the pound, weighted rate to the basis point, and a bucket cross-check that also ties exactly. Opens the email cleanly.

facts.value: CHECKED. Using Appendix B p2 (2025/26 actual): CFR £35,458k less external debt £28,232k less other long-term liabilities £0 (Appendix B p3 states 'The Council only has Finance Leases at the present time' and no finance-lease figure is printed in the Appendix B indicator tables — the amount is not material to the identity) = £7,226k internal borrowing. Appendix B p2's own printed internal-borrowing line for 2025/26 actual is £7,226k. Identity TIES EXACTLY to the pound. Alternative reading from main body p6 which reports 'Amount Borrowed (Internal and External)' £35.458m equals the CFR £35.458m by construction, i.e. the same identity restated. Internal borrowing is 20.4% of CFR (£7,226 / £35,458). Comparator 2024/25 actual: 6,513 / 37,167 = 17.5% — modest increase in internal borrowing share year-on-year, driven by the £1.000m HRA maturity not replaced plus annuity/EIP amortisation reducing external debt by £2.422m against a CFR that only fell £1.709m.

source.title: Appendix B p2 (Capital Financing Requirement and Gross Debt) and p3 (Operational Boundary text)

facts.note: Identity closes clean on Appendix B's own numbers with no ambiguity on OLTL. Under-borrowing quantum 20% is modest and worth naming in the email as scene-setting rather than as a hook in itself.

facts.value: Paper page 6, verbatim: 'While interest rates remain elevated and the Council has sufficient cashflow to allow for internal borrowing, this remains the preferred approach, with new / replacement borrowing only being considered once interest rates fall back to what the treasury advisors view as the \'long term normal level\' of around 3%.' Executive summary p2 puts the same view in slightly different words: 'The Council will continue to consider the opportunities from borrowing internally whilst current market interest rates remain relatively high, which is relevant when existing HRA loans mature and are \'replaced\'.' The trigger is set at ~3%, cited as the advisers' view of long-term normal. In-year evidence of the stance: 'a maturity loan of £1.000m was not replaced by external borrowing during the year' (p6). Also on p6, the paper cites current PWLB rates on the report date (24 July 2026) as '6% for 25 years and 5.80% for 50 years' — i.e. their trigger is a c.300bp move below the rates they see today. The same paper's Executive Summary p2 records the advisers' base-rate forecast: '3.75% in March 2026 to 3.5% in September 2027. Steady returns are therefore expected throughout 2026/27.' So the trigger sits inside the advisers' own path but not near it: their advisers are forecasting base rate at 3.5% seventeen months out, and the trigger — for long-dated PWLB — is 3%.

source.title: Main body p2 (Executive Summary) and p6 (Supporting Information)

facts.note: Distinctive across the batch. Most councils frame the borrowing decision qualitatively — 'when rates are appropriate' or 'when market conditions permit'. Tendring names a rate. Combined with the £1m HRA maturity they deliberately let run off in year and the advisers' forecast path in the same paper, this is a testable strategic position — the hook the email leads with after the reconciliation.

facts.value: Paper p6 verbatim: 'No new external borrowing or restructuring of existing debt was undertaken for General Fund or Housing Revenue Account purposes in 2025/26. Principal on HRA debt continues to be repaid each year in line with the 30-year business plan. Debt rescheduling opportunities are limited in the current economic climate with no debt rescheduling taking place in 2025/26.' Also 'No temporary borrowing from the markets was required during the year.' Movement on the external book in year: 2024/25 actual £30,654k → 2025/26 actual £28,232k = -£2,422k, being £1.000m of the HRA maturity not replaced plus £1.422m of annuity/EIP scheduled amortisation. Combined with no new drawings and no rescheduling.

source.title: Main body p6; Appendix B p2 external debt line

facts.note: Book is quiet on the debt side — consistent with the 3% trigger and the modest under-borrowing quantum. Not a hook in itself; useful backdrop.

facts.value: Paper p1 executive summary: value of investments £97.642m at 31 March 2026, average interest rate 4.378% for 2025/26, interest earned £4.949m. Paper p7: weighted average length of investments made during 2025/26 was 26 days. SONIA benchmark table (p7): Bank Rate 4.04, SONIA 30 day 4.01, SONIA 90 day 3.94, SONIA 180 day 3.87, Tendring DC 4.38. Outperformance vs SONIA 180 day = 4.378 - 3.87 = +0.508 (about 51 bp). Outperformance vs SONIA 90 day = 4.378 - 3.94 = +0.438 (about 44 bp). Outperformance vs Bank Rate average = 4.378 - 4.04 = +0.338 (about 34 bp). Paper's own framing at p8 verbatim: 'the elevated levels reflecting the timing of investments, with higher rates carried forward from the investments in early parts of the year that exceed the comparable rates for later time periods.' Placement mix at 31 March 2026 (p8): £81.000m other local authorities (82.9%); £11.500m DMO short-term (11.8%); £3.615m two Money Market Funds (3.7%); £1.527m call accounts (1.6%). Year turnover: £1.3517bn placed with DMO/UK government during the year (with £1.3522bn repaid) plus £29.120m placed with UK financial institutions. Aggregate investments £1.5077bn per Appendix A (quoted in text at p8).
facts.note: Short-book execution is solid — 26-day weighted average maturity delivering 44 bp over SONIA 90-day in a falling-rate year is what carrying earlier higher rates through short deposits should look like, and the paper is transparent about that being the mechanism. Worth naming in the email as a fair characterisation of a good year.

facts.value: Appendix B p5 maturity structure of fixed rate borrowing at 31/3/2026 (% of £28,232k external debt): under 12 months 8.58%; 12–24 months 3.86%; 24 months – 5 years 11.59%; 5–10 years 13.86%; 10–20 years 8.98%; 20–30 years 53.13%; >30 years 0.00%. Rows sum to 100.00%. At 31/3/2027 as approved by Full Council on 31 March 2026 (projected): 4.22% / 4.22% / 12.67% / 13.86% / 8.98% / 58.12% / 0.00%. The under-12-months bucket halves 8.58% → 4.22% as the £1m HRA maturity in 2025/26 is out and further scheduled maturities in 2026/27 sit on a smaller opening book. Concentration in 20–30 years grows to 58.12%. Our file (as at 2026-08-16, book £27,521,584 after 5 months of annuity/EIP amortisation): under 12 months 2 loans £1,333,333 at weighted 4.235%; 2–5 years 3 loans £28,948 at 8.639% (small annuity residuals); 5–10 years 4 loans £2,274,696 at 2.512%; 10–25 years 2 loans £9,595,467 at 2.936%; 25 years and over 6 loans £15,000,000 at 4.133%.

source.title: Appendix B p5 (Maturity Structure of Fixed Rate Borrowing)

facts.note: Long-dated concentration is typical of a stock-holding district carrying the 2012 HRA-settlement debt. 20–30 years bucket ties to the pound with our 25y+ block (£15m). Useful backdrop; not a hook.

facts.value: INDICATIVE ONLY, only the DMO can quote. Priced against the DMO's premature repayment curve (notice 314/26 PM dated 2026-08-14): balance across 17 live loans £27,521,584 (book after 5 months of 2026/27 amortisation from the year-end £28,232,443); indicative settlement £23,645,823; net indicative DISCOUNT £3,875,762 = 14.1% of principal. 10 loans below par, 7 above. Largest indicative discounts (curve-derived): PW492341 MATURITY 2052-01-15 4.10% £5,000,000 -£975,442; PW500797 EIP 2041-10-22 3.03% £5,672,483 -£574,047; PW492334 MATURITY 2056-02-15 4.15% £2,000,000 -£406,571; PW492333 MATURITY 2055-02-15 4.15% £2,000,000 -£400,899. Largest indicative premiums (small old-annuity tail at high historic coupons): PW430059 ANNUITY 2033-07-17 11.38% £8,093 +£2,097; PW414274 ANNUITY 2031-07-17 8.75% £10,510 +£1,250. Discount reflects prevailing PWLB rates being above the coupons on Tendring's long-dated maturity and EIP loans; premiums are the residual old-annuity book that is nearly amortised out.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py "TENDRING DISTRICT COUNCIL" --as-at 2026-03-31 with DMO curve notice 314/26 PM 2026-08-14

facts.note: £3.876m discount is real but modest against peers in the batch (Stroud £25.4m at 25%; Camden 19%). Fair to name as a curve-derived fact and never as advice — the Cherwell/Flintshire/Woking/Darlington disclosure template applies.

facts.value: Paper p5, verbatim: 'Although not a breach of treasury management practices, in 2025/26 there was an investment placed with another Local Authority on 20 March 2026 for £6m for the period from April 2026 to October 2026. Upon review, it was realised that the Local Authority had been added to Central Government's Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) list in February 2026, but this had not been picked up at the time of placing the deal. In order to prevent this in future, deals are now subject to authorisation / management review at the time of placing the deal instead of at the time of payment. As set out in previous discussions, there is no underlying risk associated with transactions with other Local Authorities, and this \'deal\' will be left to the \'maturity\' date in-line with the original agreement.' Counterparty LA not named in the paper.

source.title: Main body p5 (Background and Current Position)

facts.value: Paper Recommendation (c) on p2: 'approves an amendment to the Council's Treasury Management Practices that allows the maximum amount of money that can be invested per money market fund to £6.000m from the current limit of £4.000m.' Supporting text on p8: 'to increase this to £6.000m that would bring it in-line with the same level that can be invested in UK Local Authorities.' Current MMF holdings at 31/3/26 are £3.615m across the two funds combined (p8) — so £1.8m each on average, well below either the current £4m or proposed £6m per-fund cap. Increase gives operational flexibility rather than resolving a current pressure.

One property in the Commercial Investment Portfolio (Clacton, per p9). Purchase August 2017 £3.244m including stamp duty. Balance sheet value at 1 April 2025 was £2.212m; revalued to £2.136m at 31/3/26 — £0.076m impairment for 2025/26 charged then reversed through the Movement in Reserves Statement so no funding impact (p10). Rental income £0.237m in 2025/26, in line with budget, giving an annualised rate of return of approximately 7% against purchase price (p10). Original leaseholder ceased trading November 2018; property has been sublet since, with sublet expected to end in approximately 1 year (p10). 'The level of annual rent achievable from this investment property is likely to decrease based on current market expectations when the current lease expires' (p10). Cumulative revaluation history (p9–p10): purchase £3.244m → March 2026 £2.136m, a £1.108m (34%) writedown.
facts.note: One-property portfolio, transparent revaluation history, protected against forced sale in policy. Not a treasury email hook — commercial property risk is off our beat.

facts.value: Paper p6 verbatim: 'Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) rates have remained elevated alongside the base rate with the rates currently at 6% for 25 years and 5.80% for 50 years. These rates are all above the target rates set by the treasury advisors and have been since autumn 2022.' Rates cited as at the report date of 24 July 2026 (or the drafting cycle up to it). Paper does not specify standard vs certainty; does not distinguish an HRA rate.
facts.note: The paper cites its own PWLB rates. We do not have a same-date snapshot of standard-vs-certainty PWLB rates to cross-check, so we treat the paper's cited rates as their marker rather than counter them. Do not attempt a rate-move-since-strategy comparison for this paper.

facts.value: Appendix B p3: Authorised limit for borrowing 2025/26 actual £78.171m; Operational boundary £68.503m. Actual external debt at 31/3/2026 £28.232m (Appendix B p2). Headroom against Authorised Limit £78.171m − £28.232m = £49.939m; against Operational Boundary £68.503m − £28.232m = £40.271m. Compliance statement at p10 verbatim: 'During the financial year the Council operated within the treasury limits and Prudential Indicators set out in the Council's annual Treasury Strategy.' Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream (Appendix B p3): GF 1.96% actual (vs 1.06% estimate; 2.13% 2024/25 comparator); HRA 38.48% actual (vs 38.19% estimate; 43.91% 2024/25 comparator; 40.87% 2026/27 as approved). Ratio of commercial and service investments to net revenue: GF -1.46% actual (Appendix B p4). Average credit score for investments 1.02 actual for 2025/26 against 2.00 upper limit (Appendix B p5) — dominated by DMO and LA holdings which score 1.
facts.note: All indicators comfortably inside limits. Standard-shape compliance disclosure — not a hook.

officer.body:
Hi Richard,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your Treasury Management Performance report to Cabinet on 24 July, ahead of the next quarterly monitoring report that on your cycle pattern goes back to Cabinet in November. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper's clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The cross-check first, which is where we always start. Our file holds seventeen PWLB loans for Tendring totalling £28,232,443 at a weighted 3.6053%. Your Executive Summary on page 1 splits the same book as £0.112m General Fund at 6.884% plus £28.120m HRA at 3.591%. That agrees to the pound on principal and to the basis point on rate — the blended rate on your two lines works out to the same 3.6053%. The count of seventeen is ours; your paper doesn't print one. Even the shape ties: your Appendix B page 5 shows 53.13% of the book sitting in the 20–30 year bucket, and our file has £15,000,000 across six loans in the 25-year-and-over block, which is 53.13% of £28.232m to the pound. That's about as close as a reconciliation gets.

What most caught our eye is the paragraph on page 6 under Borrowing. Your treasury advisers view the long-term-normal level of rates at around 3%, and the paper is explicit that new or replacement borrowing is only being considered once rates fall back to that level. Your £1.000m HRA maturity in 2025/26 was deliberately not replaced against that trigger. That's a specific, dated view — and it sits inside the same advisers' base-rate forecast in your Executive Summary, for rates to hold at 3.75% through 2026/27 and only start falling in September 2027 to 3.5%. In other words your advisers are implicitly telling you the trigger is at least a year and a bit away on their own numbers. Most reports we've read frame the borrowing decision qualitatively — 'when rates are appropriate', 'when market conditions permit'. Naming a rate is the exception rather than the rule.

The shape that sits behind that stance is a modest under-borrowing. Your Appendix B page 2 has CFR £35.458m against external £28.232m, leaving £7.226m of internal borrowing, or 20.4% of the CFR. Not aggressive by any measure and well inside what your cash flow can carry — the identity closes to the pound on Appendix B's own numbers. Your external book fell £2.422m in the year: the £1m HRA maturity you didn't replace plus £1.422m of annuity and EIP scheduled amortisation.

The investment side is worth naming too. A 26-day weighted average maturity is short, and delivering 4.378% against your paper's own Bank Rate average of 4.04% and SONIA 90-day of 3.94% is 44 basis points ahead of SONIA 90-day. Your page 8 is transparent about the mechanism — earlier-year higher rates being carried forward through short deposits into a falling-rate year — which is exactly what a short book should do in that shape of market. £81m of the £97.6m at year end sits with other local authorities.

The /pwlb-activity page shows the sector picture that lens sits inside: how much PWLB every LA drew each month over the same period, and where on the curve it went, which is the counterpart to your decision not to draw. And /loan-analysis carries the daily reprice of your seventeen loans against the DMO's repayment curve — as of the DMO's notice 314/26 PM on 14 August, ten sit below par and seven above, with an indicative curve-derived discount of about £3.876m across the whole book, roughly 14% of principal, concentrated on your 2052 and mid-2050s maturity loans. Those are curve arithmetic — the DMO's actual quote is the only binding number and nothing about whether an early repayment would be worth doing follows from us, because that turns on replacement cost we don't model, on HRA and General Fund apportionment, on MRP treatment and on your own view. It's just a number to have visible if members ask.

One standing observation. Our liability-benchmark work at /loan-analysis is interactive and live, which matters given CIPFA has Prudential and Treasury Code updates coming. Your paper doesn't print a benchmark and most outturn reports don't. Running one against your Appendix B CFR trajectory and the internal-borrowing line would give members a single-page view of how much longer the 3% trigger has room to run before a new external draw becomes the necessary path rather than the preferred one.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is a members' course written for exactly the Cabinet audience your paper is scrutinised by; Liability benchmark modelling for treasury goes to the observation above; HRA treasury: settlement debt and self-financing speaks to the 87.8% of your CFR that sits in the HRA and the long-dated 20–30 year concentration that goes with it; and Break costs and premature repayment goes to the discount position. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
